Sanhita Vidhi Systems: The Free Tier That Costs Rs 39.75 Lakh a Month

A teaching case on AI cost-to-serve and pricing

1. Opening

On Monday 5 October 2026, Shweta Tandon arrived at the Sanhita Vidhi Systems office in Kanpur's Swaroop Nagar before the tea boy did. The head of product had one sheet of paper on her desk, printed the previous night by finance. It said that the September inference bill, paid to the model vendor for every judgment summarised and pleading drafted, had reached Rs 56.85 lakh. Subscription revenue for the same month was Rs 29.97 lakh.

The board would meet on Thursday 8 October, and Ishaan Awasthi, the founder, wanted one recommendation on the free tier of the company's AI products. The vendor's prepaid commitment renewed on 1 November, a week before Diwali, at a volume that would follow from her answer. She had three days to decide what a free advocate in Gorakhpur was entitled to.

2. Company background

Sanhita Vidhi Systems was founded in 2021 by Ishaan Awasthi, a former litigation associate at the Allahabad High Court. It sells software to district-court advocates and small law firms in Uttar Pradesh and Uttarakhand.

Its first product was a cause-list tracker and hearing diary. In March 2026 it added two AI features. Granth Saar summarises a judgment into issues, holdings and cited authorities. Vakalat Draft produces a first draft of a plaint, written statement or bail application from a short set of facts. They sit in two plans: Adaalat Free and Adaalat Pro, at Rs 999 a month excluding GST. At launch the free plan was described as "unlimited for now", and nobody had revisited the phrase.

Manupatra and SCC Online serve larger chambers; Indian Kanoon is free for search; the Digital Personal Data Protection Act shapes what client material may be uploaded. None offers a drafting assistant priced for a district practice, the space Sanhita chose. By September the product had 25,000 free monthly active advocates and 3,000 paying ones, and a team of 34.

3. The situation

Growth had come almost entirely from the free plan. Advocates share a good summary in bar-association WhatsApp groups, and twenty more juniors sign up. The vendor invoice made the counter-argument: unlike the cause-list tracker, every AI call had a price that scaled with the length of the judgment and of the draft.

Tanmay Srivastava, the engineering lead in Lucknow, built the cost model in Exhibit 1. A summary reads about 12,000 tokens and writes about 1,500; a draft reads about 8,000 and writes about 4,000. The vendor charges Rs 0.25 per 1,000 input tokens and Rs 1.00 per 1,000 output tokens. Output costs four times as much per token, yet a summary is dominated by its reading and a draft by its writing.

Usage turns Exhibit 1 into a per-user figure. The average free advocate ran 30 summaries and 4 drafts a month: 30 x Rs 4.50 = Rs 135, plus 4 x Rs 6.00 = Rs 24, or Rs 159 a month. Across 25,000 users that is Rs 39.75 lakh. Pro has a fair-use cap of 100 summaries and 20 drafts; a payer at the cap costs 100 x Rs 4.50 = Rs 450, plus 20 x Rs 6.00 = Rs 120, or Rs 570. Against Rs 999 that leaves Rs 429, a gross margin of 42.9 per cent. For 3,000 payers the bill is Rs 17.10 lakh, and Rs 39.75 lakh plus Rs 17.10 lakh is Rs 56.85 lakh. Pro is an upper bound, since not every payer reaches the cap.

In Amsterdam, Alok Nigam, the data scientist, pointed out that a summary can be produced by a much smaller model at Rs 0.05 per 1,000 input tokens and Rs 0.20 per 1,000 output tokens: 12 x 0.05 plus 1.5 x 0.20 comes to Rs 0.90, one-fifth of Rs 4.50. He warned, though, that small models sometimes cite a holding the judgment does not contain, and in law a confident wrong citation is worse than none. In Prayagraj, Sanjay Katiyar, who runs customer success, heard from High Court juniors that the free tier was the only reason they trusted the product enough to show a senior.

4. The people

Shweta Tandon, head of product, Kanpur, owns the decision and wants a plan she can defend to the board and to advocates.

Ishaan Awasthi, founder and chief executive, Kanpur, sees the free plan as distribution. The company has Rs 4.8 crore (Rs 480 lakh) in the bank and other monthly costs of Rs 38 lakh.

Tanmay Srivastava, engineering lead, Lucknow, wants hard limits before the vendor commitment renews.

Alok Nigam, data scientist, Amsterdam, wants any saving tested for citation accuracy first. Sanjay Katiyar, customer success lead, Prayagraj, wants free advocates treated as future customers.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 2 compares the options on one basis; Exhibit 3 draws it.

Option A: 30 summaries and 4 drafts. Option B: 8 summaries and 1 draft, so 8 x 4.50 + 6.00 = Rs 42. Option C: a one-time allowance of 30 summaries and 5 drafts (Rs 165) for 6,000 new trials a month. B and C are estimates.

6. The options

Option A: hold the free plan and raise money. Growth continues. The cost, per Exhibit 2, is a monthly loss of Rs 26.88 lakh after inference and a runway of 7.4 months. The free plan alone costs about three times the gross profit Pro earns (Rs 39.75 lakh against 3,000 x Rs 429, or Rs 12.87 lakh).

Option B: cap the free plan. Free advocates get 8 summaries and 1 draft a month, enough to see the product work on a real matter, not enough to run a practice on. Free inference falls from Rs 39.75 lakh to Rs 10.50 lakh, a little over a quarter of the old figure, and total inference drops by Rs 29.25 lakh. The company turns marginally positive, with a runway of 13.5 months. The risk is that payers fall as the WhatsApp sharing cools; metering must be built before 1 November.

Option C: end the free plan and offer a trial. Each new advocate gets a one-time allowance and then must pay. Trial inference is Rs 9.90 lakh, but Exhibit 2 assumes payers fall to 2,100, so revenue falls to Rs 20.98 lakh and the result is still a loss of Rs 0.89 lakh.

7. Questions for discussion

1. Reconstruct the Rs 159 free-user cost and the Rs 570 Pro cost from Exhibit 1. Which call type drives each?

2. Why is Pro's gross margin a healthy 42.9 per cent while the company margin under Option A is -89.7 per cent?

3. Option C has a smaller inference bill than B yet a worse result. Which assumption drives this, and what evidence would you want?

4. Which option would you take to the board, and what would make you change course?

8. A note for the learner

When every use costs money to serve, a free tier is not a marketing discount but a variable cost, and it must be sized like one. The discipline is to express usage in cost units (tokens, then rupees per call, then rupees per user), to compare the cost of free users with the gross profit paying users generate, and to decide how much acquisition spend the business will fund each month.

One defensible path is Option B. It cuts the largest and least productive cost, Rs 39.75 lakh a month, by about three-quarters while keeping the product visible to every advocate who might later pay. It is reversible: a cap of 8 summaries can be lifted if conversion holds, whereas an ended free plan is hard to bring back. And the cap sets a ceiling on cost per free user (Rs 42) rather than hoping usage falls.

A strong answer adds three conditions. First, track paying users weekly against the 3,000 baseline, and treat a fall towards 2,100, the level Option C assumed, as the signal to reopen the decision. Second, have Alok test the small model on summaries (Rs 0.90 against Rs 4.50), releasing it only if citation accuracy matches; drafts stay on the stronger model. Third, renew the vendor commitment at the volume Option B implies, not Option A's. Weaker answers defend "unlimited for now" or abolish the free plan without computing what the arithmetic supports.

AI Cost-to-Serve and Pricing

Can we afford a free tier when every use costs inference? A working explainer for the product manager who has just discovered that a friendly feature has a bill attached to it.

1. A Friday afternoon at Rasoi Sahayak

On the second Friday of March 2026, Priya Raman, head of product for the recipe and meal-planning app Rasoi Sahayak, opened a spreadsheet that Finance had sent her twenty minutes before a leadership review and felt the particular cold that comes from a number that does not match the story in your head. The line item was labelled, without ceremony, "AI Assistant – inference (Feb)": $41,900. Converted at roughly ₹87 to the dollar, that was ₹36.5 lakh for a single month, for a feature that had shipped nine months earlier as a small, cheerful addition to a free app – a chat box where a home cook could ask "what can I make with paneer, one capsicum and leftover rice" and get a plan back in a few seconds.

Rasoi Sahayak had 2.4 million monthly active users in February, of whom 68,000 paid ₹149 a month for an ad-free, unlimited tier – a conversion rate of 2.8%, which Priya's board considered respectable for a consumer cooking app. Subscription revenue for the month had been just over ₹1 crore. The AI assistant, which had been pitched internally as a low-cost delighter, was now consuming inference spend equivalent to roughly a third of that revenue, and it was overwhelmingly the free users driving it: an internal cut showed that 520,000 free users had used the assistant at least once in February, compared with a much smaller, much heavier-using paid cohort whose usage the subscription price already covered several times over. The review was in four days. Priya's task was not to panic, and not to simply switch the feature off – it had become the single most-cited reason people gave for downloading the app in App Store reviews – but to understand, quickly and precisely, why a feature that felt weightless to build had turned out to have a marginal cost that scaled with every tap, and to bring the board a plan rather than an apology.

2. The idea: cost-to-serve when marginal cost is not zero

AI cost-to-serve is the per-use, variable cost of running an AI feature for one customer interaction – principally the fee an inference provider charges for the tokens a large language model reads and writes to answer a single request – tracked against what that interaction is allowed to earn under the pricing plan the customer sits on. It is a narrower, sharper cousin of the older idea of "cost of goods sold" in software: for two decades, software people were trained to think of the marginal cost of serving one more user as close enough to zero to ignore, because a server handling one more login or one more page view barely noticed the difference. Generative AI features break that assumption, because every response is manufactured on demand by a model that is billed, almost always, by the token – a token being roughly three-quarters of an English word, the unit in which an inference provider such as an API-based model vendor counts both what you send it and what it sends back. The idea of cost-to-serve as a first-class product metric, distinct from aggregate cloud spend, entered product management vocabulary quickly between 2023 and 2025, as teams that had shipped chat-based features on top of hosted models discovered – usually the way Priya did – that their COGS line had stopped being a rounding error and started being a line the CFO asked about by name.

The sentence Priya could say in the boardroom without sounding glib is this: every AI response we send has a real, calculable cost before a single rupee of revenue touches it, and a free tier only works if we know that number and design around it on purpose. That sentence matters because it reframes the free tier from a marketing decision into an engineering-and-pricing decision made jointly, which is precisely the discipline that traditional software freemium, running on marginal cost close to zero, never demanded.

3. How it actually works

The mechanics sit on four moving parts, and the second and third are the ones practitioners most often leave implicit until a bill forces them into the open. First, every request to a model carries an input component – the text the model must read before it can respond – and every reply carries an output component, and providers price these separately, with output tokens typically costing several times more than input tokens because generating text is computationally heavier than reading it. Second, the input a model actually reads on any given turn is almost never just what the user typed: it includes a system prompt (instructions telling the model how to behave), any retrieved context (in Rasoi Sahayak's case, matching recipes and nutrition data pulled from a database), and, critically, the entire prior conversation, because most chat interfaces are stateless underneath and must resend the full history with every new turn for the model to "remember" what was said. Third, teams choose a model tier – a compact, cheaper model or a larger, more capable "frontier" model – and that choice, made once by an engineer trying to get good recipe suggestions, quietly sets the per-token price for every future conversation. Fourth, the total monthly bill is this per-call cost multiplied across a funnel: total users, times the share who touch the feature, times sessions per user, times turns per session – a multiplication chain in which each stage looks harmless and the product of all four does not.

4. A worked example, line by line

Rasoi Sahayak had built its assistant on a frontier-tier model priced, illustratively, at $2.50 per million input tokens and $10.00 per million output tokens – chosen because an earlier, cheaper model had produced recipe combinations that were occasionally inedible, and the team, reasonably, prioritised quality over cost at launch. A typical session had three back-and-forth turns, and because the app resent the growing conversation each time, the input tokens were not simply three times a single turn's input – they compounded. The table below shows the arithmetic exactly as Priya's data scientist reconstructed it.

Round that to $0.0161 per session. Multiply it by the funnel: 520,000 free users engaged with the assistant in February, averaging five sessions each. That is 2.6 million sessions, and 2.6 million times $0.0161 lands at $41,860 – which is, to the dollar Finance's number came close to, exactly the bill that had alarmed the board. No single stage of that chain looks reckless in isolation: a fifth-of-a-cent session multiplied by a large, engaged free user base simply becomes a five-figure monthly cost, because multiplication does not care how small the first number felt.

Now change one input, holding everything else constant, to see how much of the number is a genuine feature-of-use cost and how much is a model-choice cost. Suppose Rasoi Sahayak's engineers swap the frontier model for a compact model priced at $0.15 per million input tokens and $0.60 per million output tokens – roughly a sixteenth of the price on both counts – and, because the compact model is smaller, they also trim the retrieved context slightly. The session cost falls to roughly $0.00097, and the same 2.6 million monthly sessions now cost about $2,520 rather than $41,900: a reduction of more than 94%, achieved with zero change in how many people use the feature or how often. The lesson embedded in that second pass is the single most important operating fact in this whole topic: for a chat-style AI feature, the choice of which model answers a given request is usually a larger lever on cost-to-serve than anything a product manager can do to reduce how much people use the product – and unlike usage, it is a lever the team controls entirely on its own.

A fifth of a cent per session is not a cost you can ignore – it is a cost you have not yet multiplied.

5. The nuances a learner must hold onto

Cost per call is not cost per user, and neither is cost per outcome

It is tempting to report a single tidy figure – "our AI feature costs half a cent a call" – and stop there, but three different denominators answer three different questions. Cost per call tells an engineer whether one request is efficient. Cost per user tells a product manager whether a pricing tier can absorb a typical customer's usage. Cost per outcome – for instance, cost per completed meal plan that a user actually cooked, rather than abandoned mid-conversation – tells you whether the spend is buying anything of value at all. A feature can look cheap on the first measure and ruinous on the second if a small share of users drive most of the volume, and a team that only ever reports the first number is, whether it intends to or not, hiding the number that would worry the board.

Usage inside a free tier is almost never evenly distributed

Averages mislead here more than almost anywhere else in product economics. In Rasoi Sahayak's data, the top 5% of free users who touched the assistant accounted for nearly 40% of all sessions, because a small cohort of enthusiastic home cooks used it daily while the median user tried it once and moved on. A cost-to-serve plan built around the average session count per user will systematically underestimate the bill, because the bill is driven by the tail, not the middle.

List price per token is a moving target, and it moves in both directions

Inference prices from model providers have generally fallen over time as competition and efficiency gains compound, and it is reasonable to expect the same capability to cost less next year than it costs today. But product teams routinely spend that saving before it arrives, by upgrading to a newer, more capable – and more expensive – model, adding retrieved context, or supporting longer conversations, all in the name of quality. Falling per-token prices and rising per-session costs can and do coexist, and a team that tracks only the provider's published price list, rather than its own realised cost per session over time, will miss this entirely.

Free trials and freemium carry this risk very differently

A time-boxed free trial exposes a company to inference cost for a bounded window per user and then either converts or ends it; an always-on free tier, by contrast, is an open-ended liability that renews every month for as long as the user stays, which is exactly why the learning objective behind this topic singles out generous free tiers as the dangerous case – the exposure compounds with retention rather than expiring with it.

Caching and retrieval design change the input side more than most teams expect

Many of the input tokens in a typical call – the system prompt, and often the retrieved context – repeat across calls and can be cached or shortened by an engineering team without touching the user experience at all, which is a very different remedy from restricting usage and is usually the first place a mature team looks before it ever discusses caps or pricing changes.

Cost-to-serve is not the same thing as total cloud spend

A company's overall cloud bill includes storage, standard compute, monitoring and dozens of line items that have nothing to do with any one feature. Cost-to-serve is a feature-specific, usage-linked slice of that bill, and conflating the two – blaming an AI feature for a cost spike that is actually a database migration, or crediting it for a saving that came from an unrelated infrastructure change – is one of the most common analytical errors in this space.

A low cost-to-serve does not prove the feature is worth building

Even a nearly-free AI feature can be a bad investment if it does not move retention, conversion or willingness to pay; conversely, an expensive feature that meaningfully lifts paid conversion can be an excellent investment at a cost-to-serve that would look alarming in isolation. The metric answers "can we afford this at this volume," not "should we build this at all," and treating it as a complete verdict is a category error.

The number always needs a "so what" tied to a specific tier

A cost-to-serve figure means nothing until it is set against what that specific tier is allowed to earn. $0.016 a session is trivial against a ₹149 unlimited paid plan and genuinely threatening against a free tier that earns nothing directly at all – the same cost, two entirely different verdicts, depending purely on which side of the pricing wall the user sits.

6. How this looks different by business model and by company stage

In a high-volume consumer product like Rasoi Sahayak, the free tier exists to build habit and to generate the word-of-mouth and app-store visibility that a young consumer brand cannot otherwise afford, so the AI feature's cost-to-serve has to be pushed toward near-zero through model choice and caching rather than recovered through price, because consumer users have very low willingness to pay for a single feature and will simply churn if asked to pay for something that used to be free. In a business-to-business product, the calculus is friendlier: a hypothetical enterprise compliance-copilot vendor, call it Rezonate Cloud, selling a document-review assistant at ₹15,000 per seat per month to corporate legal teams, can let a seat generate fifty AI sessions a day and still spend only a small single-digit percentage of that seat's revenue on inference, because B2B pricing is negotiated against a much higher willingness to pay and usage caps, when needed, are enforced against a known, named buyer rather than an anonymous free signup. In a marketplace model – imagine a logistics and ride marketplace, Raahgiri Mobility, offering an AI support chatbot to both drivers and riders – the right question is not whether the chatbot breaks even on its own, but whether the AI-assisted resolution of a support issue or a pricing dispute increases completed transactions and take-rate revenue on the other side of the marketplace by more than the inference it costs, which is a two-sided unit-economics question that a purely one-sided SaaS mental model will get wrong.

Company stage matters just as much as business model. An early-stage team, like Rasoi Sahayak nine months into this feature, typically pays list price for inference, lacks the engineering time to build caching or model-routing infrastructure, and often accepts a bruising cost-to-serve for a period deliberately, as the price of proving that the feature drives retention before investing in efficiency – provided someone sets an explicit ceiling and a date to revisit it. A large, mature platform, by contrast, can negotiate committed-use discounts with inference providers, can afford to build and maintain a "router" that sends easy requests to a cheap model and only hard requests to an expensive one, and can spread the fixed cost of that engineering work across a volume so large that the same per-session economics that terrify a startup barely register as a rounding error on its income statement.

7. Common mistakes

Mistake one: tracking cost against total registered users instead of active feature users. The symptom is a Finance chart that shows cost per user falling steadily as the app grows, which looks reassuring right up until the total bill outpaces revenue anyway. The underlying error is a denominator mismatch – dividing a cost that is driven by active feature usage by a headcount that includes millions of people who never opened the feature. The cheapest diagnostic is to recompute the same ratio using only users who triggered at least one call that month; if that number is rising while the "per registered user" number is falling, the team is looking at a comforting illusion.

Mistake two: not counting retries and regenerations as separate calls. The symptom is a cost forecast that blows past its estimate right after a seemingly cosmetic UI change, such as adding a "regenerate this plan" button. The underlying misunderstanding is treating "one user action" as "one billed call," when a single visible interaction can trigger two, three or more model calls if the interface allows retries, reformulation, or a background quality check. The cheapest diagnostic is to instrument and log calls per session as its own distribution, not merely sessions per user.

Mistake three: budgeting from the average user rather than the tail. The symptom is a monthly bill that repeatedly exceeds a forecast built from what looks like a careful per-user estimate. The underlying misunderstanding, as noted in the nuances above, is that AI feature usage inside a free tier is heavy-tailed, so an average grossly understates the true bill. The cheapest diagnostic is a simple percentile breakdown – what share of total sessions come from the top 1% and top 5% of users – run once and revisited whenever the user base changes composition.

Mistake four: assuming falling model prices will fix the problem without anyone doing anything. The symptom is a team that defers a pricing or caps decision on the theory that "inference will get cheaper," and then finds the bill unchanged or higher a year later. The underlying misunderstanding is ignoring that the same team, in that same year, usually upgrades the model, lengthens the context, or adds a new capability that eats the savings. The cheapest diagnostic is tracking realised cost per session over time on a chart placed next to, not instead of, the provider's published token price.

8. What good looks like

Consider, by contrast, how the fictional Rezonate Cloud approached the same category of decision when it added an AI drafting assistant to its enterprise contract-management product. Before shipping to a single customer, its product and engineering leads had already agreed on three things: a target cost-to-serve per seat per month, expressed as a fixed percentage of the seat's list price, not as an absolute dollar figure that would need renegotiating every time the price list changed; a two-tier model-routing design in which the majority of routine requests – clause lookups, formatting, summarisation – were served by an inexpensive model, with only genuinely complex drafting tasks escalated to the frontier model, a design decided in advance rather than retrofitted under pressure; and a monthly cost-per-seat dashboard, reviewed by product and finance together, so that a cost anomaly would surface within weeks rather than being discovered by an accountant during a quarterly close. The result was not a cost-to-serve of zero – enterprise customers used the assistant heavily, precisely because it was good – but a cost-to-serve that stayed, quarter after quarter, inside a known and defensible band relative to revenue, which meant no leadership meeting was ever an ambush. The discipline was not cleverness so much as sequencing: decide the ceiling and the routing logic before scale arrives, not after a bill forces the conversation.

9. What Priya decided, and where to go from here

Priya's recommendation to the board on Tuesday had three parts, each traceable to the arithmetic above. First, the assistant would move, for free-tier users only, onto the compact model for the first two turns of any conversation, escalating to the frontier model only if the compact model's own confidence score came back low – a routing rule modelled directly on Rezonate Cloud's approach, projected to cut the free-tier bill by roughly 80% based on the second-pass calculation her team had already run. Second, free-tier sessions would carry a visible, generous but finite monthly cap – ten sessions, well above what the median free user consumed but a real ceiling against the heavy tail identified in section 5 – framed to users not as a restriction but as "assistant credits," with unlimited access positioned as one clear reason, among several, to upgrade. Third, and least visible to any user, Finance and product would jointly own a monthly cost-per-active-feature-user dashboard going forward, so that the next surprise, if there was one, would surface as a trend line in April rather than as a spreadsheet on a Friday afternoon in March. None of the three decisions required Priya to apologise for having shipped a feature people loved; all three required her to accept that a feature whose marginal cost is not zero has to be designed, from the first architecture decision onward, with pricing and infrastructure sitting at the same table as delight.

The natural next things to study from here are token economics in more technical depth – how context windows, caching and quantisation actually move the per-token price an engineering team pays – and the broader question of pricing and usage caps for AI features once a company has more than one AI-powered capability competing for the same cost budget. Two questions worth sitting with in the meantime: if your product's free tier could not fall back to a cheaper model without anyone noticing the difference in quality, would you know, today, by how much your costs would change? And when a feature's cost genuinely does scale with delight rather than with waste, at what point does capping it stop being prudent unit economics and start being the thing that makes the product worse than the version a less careful competitor is willing to ship?

Illustrative figures throughout – model prices, token counts and conversion rates – are order-of-magnitude teaching estimates, not quoted vendor pricing, and are chosen to make the arithmetic transparent rather than to describe any single real product.

Vaani Audit Systems: Four Unit Costs, One Invoice

A case on AI cost-to-serve and pricing. Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar (Aurangabad), October 2026.

1. Sunday night, 18 October 2026

By Sunday night Prachi Sonawane had three versions of one slide open — Cost to serve, one agent seat, September 2026 — and could not decide which was true. On the first the number was Rs 900. On the second, Rs 1,470. On the third, Rs 1,761. Nobody had erred: each was computed by a colleague who could defend it to an auditor, from the same invoices and the same September volumes.

Monday's pricing committee would settle the price of Awaaz Score for the 2027 financial year; on Friday 30 October the board would see a gross margin; on 31 December, Tatva Life Assurance would order 900 more agent seats for its Amravati floor at a price its procurement team believed locked to 31 March 2029. The company did know what its AI product cost. It knew in four ways, and the four answers did not sit inside one business.

2. How Vaani got here

Eknath Jadhav founded the company in Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar in 2019, after eleven years in insurance tele-sales and collections operations spent signing quality-assurance reports he knew to be fiction: a team listening to 2 per cent of calls, and a scorecard built on that sample. His first product, Vaani QA Sampler, was rules-based keyword spotting at Rs 350 per agent seat per month with unlimited volume, defensible because scanning one more recording cost nothing.

Two decisions from then constrain October 2026. The first is the metric: when Awaaz Score replaced the keyword engine in January 2026 — transcribing and scoring every recorded call against a rubric covering mis-selling language, mandatory disclosures and abusive-recovery breaches — it inherited the per-seat, unlimited-volume shape unchanged.

The second was the Tatva Life deal of January 2026. Tatva Life Assurance, a private life insurer in Thane, took 2,400 seats at Rs 1,600 a seat a month for 36 months, price locked to 31 March 2029. Two clauses were the cost of winning it: Tatva's quality floor was stood down and Vaani took 30 displaced auditors onto its own payroll for twelve months from 1 May 2026; and a Rs 600 lakh annual committed spend with the frontier-model vendor, signed on 1 April 2026 for a 40 per cent discount off list, was sized on the assumption that the Tatva floor would fill it.

3. The industry

The demand side was unambiguous. IRDAI had spent three years pressing insurers on mis-selling and on the persistency of telephone-sold policies, and its Protection of Policyholders' Interests framework had made the audit trail of a sales call a board matter; on collections, the Reserve Bank's Fair Practices Code and its recovery-agent guidance set out what an agent may say, whom they may call and when; TRAI governed dialling; and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governed the recordings. A floor sampling 2 per cent of its calls was indefensible.

Uniphore and Gnani.ai, both Indian, and Observe.AI sold conversational intelligence into contact centres; NICE and Verint sold the incumbent global stack. Almost all priced per seat, which was Vaani's comfort and its trap. Two Vaani accounts were Manila operations reselling its output per account serviced, and Tatva's minority shareholder, Alpstein Assekuranz of Zurich, read the monthly breach reports.

4. What happened, and what turned out to be wrong

Between April and September 2026 seats grew from 3,100 to 8,200 across 41 accounts and annualised recurring revenue reached about Rs 15.7 crore. Every month the seat target was met and the invoice came in above forecast.

April: the commitment looked reckless in the wrong direction. At April's 93.0 lakh billed audio minutes the inference draw was Rs 13.95 lakh; held flat for twelve months that would have used Rs 167.40 lakh of a Rs 600 lakh pool and forfeited Rs 432.60 lakh. Kapil Kshirsagar, the chief financial officer, called it the company's largest single exposure in May. By September it was the only reason the numbers looked as good as they did.

14 August: the model change. Zoya Pathak moved scoring from the vendor's standard tier to a reasoning-capable tier, complete by 31 August.
