AI Cost-to-Serve and Pricing

What a per-use marginal cost really does to a pricing architecture — distributions, options and the seams between teams

This page assumes you already know the arithmetic: that tokens are billed in and out, that conversation history compounds, that model choice is usually the largest single lever, and that a fifth of a cent multiplied by a few million sessions is a line item the CFO will ask about by name. What follows is the argument that begins where that arithmetic ends. The claim is simple to state and uncomfortable to act on: cost-to-serve is not a number, it is a distribution with a fat right tail, and every pricing commitment you make is a short option written against that distribution and against your own product roadmap. Teams that manage the mean lose money slowly and then quickly. Teams that manage the tail and keep their commitments repriceable survive the next model upgrade.

1. Two decisions, September 2026

On 9 September 2026, in a converted textile mill in Pune that now houses about ninety engineers, Aditi Kulkarni, VP of Product at Bhanwar Systems, was handed a chart she had asked for and immediately wished she had asked for six months earlier. Bhanwar sells an AI code-review and test-generation agent to engineering teams: you connect a repository, and on every pull request the agent reads the diff, walks the surrounding files, writes a review, and — on the paid plans — proposes a patch and a test. The company had grown the way product-led companies are supposed to grow. Individual developers and open-source projects used it free; teams of five or more paid $29 per developer per month; a mid-market plan at $79 added the patch-writing agent and priority runs. In August, Bhanwar had 41,000 free repositories connected, 3,900 paying seats, and monthly recurring revenue of about $214,000, or roughly ₹1.86 crore.

The chart showed inference spend by plan for the preceding four months, but the line that mattered was not the total. It was the ninety-ninth percentile of cost per review. In May, when the agent still worked in a single pass — read the diff, write the comment — the median review cost $0.011 and the ninety-ninth percentile cost $0.09: an eight-fold spread, annoying but bounded. In July, Bhanwar's engineering team had shipped what the release notes called “deep review”: the agent could now decide, on its own, to open additional files, run a static analyser, re-read its own draft and revise it. Quality metrics improved sharply; the share of reviews a developer marked helpful rose from 47% to 71%. The median cost per review rose only to $0.019. The ninety-ninth percentile rose to $2.40. One review, on a 4,000-line refactor in a Django monorepo belonging to a free user in Indore, had cost $31.70, because the agent had opened one hundred and forty files and rewritten its draft eleven times before deciding it was done.

Aditi's problem was not the $31.70. It was what the $31.70 implied. Bhanwar's free tier had been priced — in the loose sense that anything free is priced — against a world in which the worst possible review cost nine cents. The company had, without any meeting at which this was decided, replaced a bounded liability with an unbounded one, and had done it in a release that everyone agreed was the best work the team had ever shipped. The board meeting was on 26 September. The growth investor on the board had already sent a one-line email: “What is gross margin on the paid plans, excluding and including free-tier support cost? Please show incremental, not blended.”

Eight hundred kilometres south, in a building off Bannerghatta Road in Bengaluru, Dr. Ramesh Iyer, chief product officer of Bhrigu Imaging Systems, was reading a contract he had signed twenty-two months earlier and did not enjoy the experience. Bhrigu makes a portable chest-X-ray unit with an onboard triage model: the device flags suspected tuberculosis, pneumothorax and pleural effusion in about forty seconds, and a second-stage model — which runs in Bhrigu's cloud, not on the device — drafts a structured radiology report that a qualified radiologist reviews and signs. The device is sold outright to hospital chains and to state health missions at ₹11.4 lakh per unit, with a five-year software-and-support contract at ₹96,000 per unit per year. The contract Ramesh was re-reading covered 340 units deployed across two state tuberculosis-elimination programmes, and it specified, in a schedule drafted before anyone at Bhrigu had heard the phrase cost-to-serve, “unlimited AI-assisted report generation for the contract term.”

When the contract was signed in November 2024, the report-drafting model was a fine-tuned open-weights model Bhrigu hosted itself on two rented GPUs, and the fully loaded cost per report was about ₹0.90. Then two things happened. Screening volumes rose — the whole point of a portable unit is that it goes to villages, and in the districts where it went, it did between 180 and 240 studies a day rather than the 60 Bhrigu had modelled. And in early 2026 Bhrigu's clinical team, under pressure from a radiologist advisory panel and from the device's regulatory file, moved the report drafter to a much larger multimodal model that read the image directly rather than reading the first-stage model's labels. Report acceptance by the reviewing radiologist — the share of drafts signed with no substantive edit — went from 58% to 84%. The cost per report went to ₹7.10. At 340 units running an average of 150 studies a day, twenty-six days a month, Bhrigu was spending ₹94 lakh a month on inference against contracted software revenue of ₹27.2 lakh a month from the same units. Ramesh could not raise the price; the contract ran to 2029. He could not route to the cheaper model; the larger model was named in the CDSCO submission and in the clinical validation report, and swapping it was a change-control event requiring revalidation, not a configuration flag. He could not reduce volume; higher volume was the programme's explicit public-health objective and the thing everyone at Bhrigu was proud of.

Put the two cases side by side, because the rest of this page is an argument about what they have in common. Aditi has a cost distribution whose tail escaped while the mean stayed calm. Ramesh has a mean that moved and a price that cannot. Neither made a stupid decision. Both shipped a quality improvement that their users and their own metrics validated. In both cases the damage was done not by the inference bill but by a commitment — a free tier, a five-year fixed-price contract — that had been written when the cost function looked different and that contained no mechanism for noticing that it had changed.

2. The idea, stated precisely, and the schools that disagree about it

Define the object carefully, because most of the confusion in this field is definitional. Cost-to-serve for an AI feature is the expected variable cost of delivering one unit of customer-visible value, conditional on the quality level the product has committed to, measured against the revenue that unit is permitted to earn under the plan the customer occupies. Four parts of that sentence do real work. Expected means we are talking about a random variable, not a constant. One unit of customer-visible value means the denominator is an outcome — a reviewed pull request, a signed radiology report — not a model call, because the number of model calls per outcome is itself a variable the system chooses. Conditional on the quality level committed to means cost is endogenous: you do not have a cost, you have a cost-quality curve, and naming a cost without naming the quality point is like quoting a price without a currency. Permitted to earn under the plan means the metric is meaningless until it is attached to a tier, because the same 1.6 cents is trivial against an enterprise seat and existential against a free signup.

The intellectual history is older and less novel than the field's self-image suggests, with one genuinely new element at the end. Activity-based costing — the discipline of tracing overhead to the activities that actually consume it, rather than smearing it across units by a volume-based allocation — was formalised by Robin Cooper and Robert Kaplan at Harvard in the late 1980s, and the phrase “cost-to-serve” enters the management literature through logistics and consumer-goods distribution in the 1990s, where it answered a question that will feel familiar: why is this large, prestigious customer, who buys in volume at a good price, unprofitable? The answer was almost always that the customer consumed a disproportionate share of activities — emergency deliveries, custom packing, returns — that the price did not price. Separately, the economics of capacity-constrained utilities gave us peak-load pricing, developed by Marcel Boiteux at Électricité de France in the 1950s, which established the principle that when marginal cost varies with time and load, a single flat tariff subsidises the peak user at the expense of the average one. Airlines industrialised the same insight as yield management in the 1980s.

Software then spent twenty-five years forgetting all of it, for a defensible reason. Carl Shapiro and Hal Varian's Information Rules (1998) codified the doctrine that information goods have high fixed and negligible marginal cost, and that the pricing consequences — versioning, bundling, differential pricing, and giving things away to build a network — follow from that one fact. The doctrine was substantially true. Cloud infrastructure from 2006 onward put a small, real marginal cost back into software, but it was small enough that the SaaS metrics canon treated gross margin as a solved problem: 75–85% was normal, a company below 70% was assumed to have a services attach problem, and product managers were not expected to think about COGS at all. An entire generation of pricing craft — freemium, unlimited plans, seat-based pricing, land-and-expand — was built on the premise that the cost of an additional user was rounding error.

What generative AI changed is not merely that the marginal cost is bigger. It is that the supplier decides how much you consume. When a user loads a web page, the page's cost is determined by the page. When a user asks a model a question, the cost is determined by how much the model chooses to read, think and write in response — a stochastic quantity, drawn from a distribution the model provider can and does change under you with each release, and which your own quality-seeking engineers will deliberately push rightward whenever they can trade tokens for accuracy. That is the genuinely new thing, and it is why the old cost-to-serve literature, useful as it is, does not transfer cleanly. A logistics manager's cost-to-serve varied because customers behaved differently. An AI product manager's cost-to-serve varies because customers behave differently and because the production process is itself non-deterministic and quality-elastic.

Four schools have formed around what to do about this, and they are not reconcilable by a sensible-sounding synthesis. Each is held by serious practitioners with real evidence. The table below states the proposition each school would sign and the one it would refuse, which is a more honest way of distinguishing them than summarising their rhetoric.

It is worth being explicit that the disagreement is partly empirical and partly about time horizon, and that the empirical part is testable. The land-and-deflate school rests on a real observation: the price of a fixed capability — say, the quality of output that a flagship model produced in early 2024 — has indeed collapsed, often by more than 90% within eighteen months, as smaller models trained on better data caught up and as inference stacks improved. The margin-restoration school rests on an equally real observation, which the first school tends to elide: almost no product team holds capability fixed. They spend the deflation on quality, and the cost per completed task has in many product categories been flat or rising, because reasoning-style models consume far more output tokens per answer and agentic architectures consume many calls per task. Both observations are true. Which one governs your P&L depends entirely on whether your organisation is capable of not upgrading — which is a question about your culture, not about the model market. Aditi's team spent eighteen months of price deflation in a single July release and did not notice they had done it.

3. Mechanics in depth: the identity, the distribution, and the four second-order effects

Start with the identity, because everything else is a commentary on it. The variable cost of one delivered outcome is

Coutcome = k × (1 + r) × [ Tin × pineff + Tout × pout ]

where k is the number of model calls the system makes per delivered outcome, r is the rate of retries, regenerations and failed calls that still bill, T are token counts, and pineff is the effective input price after cache hits — if a share h of input tokens are served from a prompt cache billed at a fraction f of list, then pineff = pin(1 − h + hf). The working explainer for this topic treats k as one and r as a footnote. That is precisely the simplification that broke at Bhanwar. In an agentic architecture, k is not a constant; it is a random variable whose distribution is determined by a policy inside the model, and its upper tail is bounded only by whatever loop guard your engineers remembered to write. Most of the difference between a competent and an expert treatment of AI cost-to-serve lives in the two terms, k and r, that the identity's simple form hides.

Work it through on Bhanwar's actual numbers. The shallow reviewer made one call with about 6,000 input tokens (system prompt, repository conventions file, the diff) and produced about 450 output tokens, on a mid-tier model priced illustratively at $1.10 per million input and $4.40 per million output. The deep reviewer makes a variable number of calls, each of which carries the accumulated transcript of everything it has read so far — the quadratic problem, because step n re-reads the output of steps 1 through n−1 — and it uses a reasoning-style configuration that emits hidden intermediate tokens billed as output. Table 2 lays the two architectures side by side at the median and at the ninety-ninth percentile.

Now the part that almost no one models and everyone eventually pays for. Because k is a random variable with a heavy right tail, the mean cost is not a summary of the cost — it is dominated by the tail. In Bhanwar's July data, the top 1% of reviews consumed 34% of total inference spend, and the top 0.1% consumed 14%. That is not an anomaly to be cleaned out of the data; it is the shape of the data, and it has a specific structural cause. Agentic cost per task is roughly multiplicative in the number of steps and in the context each step carries, and the product of two right-skewed quantities is a lognormal-ish variable whose mean sits far above its median. Anyone who forecasts an agentic feature's bill by multiplying a median cost by a volume will underestimate it by a factor that grows with scale, because larger samples reach further into the tail.

The first practical consequence is that a usage cap is not primarily a demand-management device; it is a truncation of the cost distribution, and its economics should be computed as one. If X is the per-user monthly cost and you impose a hard ceiling at K, your expected cost per user becomes E[min(X, K)], and the saving is E[X] − E[min(X, K)] — entirely concentrated in the users above K. Table 3 works this for Bhanwar's free tier using the actual August distribution of monthly cost per free repository. The result is the single most useful number in this whole exercise, and it is a number most teams never compute: a cap placed at the ninety-fifth percentile of usage removes 38% of the free-tier bill while changing the experience of one free user in twenty, and a cap at the ninety-ninth percentile still removes 21% while touching one in a hundred.

The second consequence is that the cap has a natural reference point that is not arbitrary: the value of a free user. Bhanwar's data showed that a free repository converted to a paid seat at 1.9% within twelve months, that an average converted account carried 4.3 seats at $29, and that gross retention on paid seats was 88% annually, implying an expected gross profit per converted account of roughly $2,400 over three years at the paid plan's own contribution margin. Multiply: expected value of a free repository = 0.019 × $2,400 = $45.60, less the inference cost it will itself consume. If the company is willing to spend a third of the expected value on acquiring it — a deliberately conservative fraction, since free repositories also generate referral and brand value that this calculation ignores — then the justified lifetime inference budget per free repository is about $15, or roughly $1.25 a month against an actual mean of $1.95. That single comparison reframes Aditi's decision. The free tier is not catastrophically mispriced; it is about 55% over budget, and the overage is concentrated in a few hundred repositories. A cap at p95 brings the mean to $1.21 and the tier back inside its own justification without touching nineteen users in twenty.

The four second-order effects

Routing is not free, and the escalation arithmetic has a break-even. The standard advice — send easy requests to a cheap model, escalate hard ones — is sound but is usually stated without the condition under which it fails. If a cheap model costs c1, the frontier model costs c2, and the cheap model's output is accepted on a fraction a of requests, then a naive escalate-on-failure router costs c1 + (1 − a)c2 per request, which beats always-frontier only when a > c1/c2. With Bhanwar's numbers — a compact model at $0.0061 per review against the deep reviewer at $0.0591 — the threshold acceptance rate is 10.3%, which sounds trivially easy to clear and mostly is. But the formula omits three costs that are real: the classifier or confidence check that decides whether to escalate is itself an inference call; a wrong escalation decision that ships a bad review to a paying customer has a support and churn cost far above the token saving; and the latency of a failed cheap attempt is added to, not shared with, the frontier attempt, which on a user-facing feature is itself a quality regression. Aditi's team found, when they instrumented this properly, that their first router had an acceptance rate of 61% and looked like a triumph, but that the escalated 39% were systematically the reviews on the largest and most commercially important repositories — so the router was saving money on the requests that mattered least and adding two seconds of latency to the requests that mattered most.

Efficiency gains are spent internally before they are banked. The generalised form of Jevons' paradox inside a product organisation is this: when the unit cost of a capability falls, the organisation's internal standard for how lavishly to use that capability rises to consume the saving, because the engineer who proposes to use twice as much context to fix a known quality complaint is making an obviously good argument and the engineer who proposes to keep the bill flat is making an abstract one. The empirical signature is a chart in which the provider's published price per million tokens falls monotonically and the company's realised cost per completed task is flat. Expert teams counter this not with exhortation but with structure: an explicit per-outcome cost budget that is treated as a product requirement of the same standing as a latency budget, breached only with the same seniority of approval. Bhrigu had a latency budget for the on-device model — forty seconds, written into the product spec — and no cost budget for the cloud model, which is exactly why the device stayed fast and the cloud bill did not stay small.

Caching, batching and committed capacity convert variable cost into fixed cost, and that is a strategic choice, not a procurement one. A prompt cache turns repeated input into a near-free input, which rewards architectures that put the stable material first and the variable material last — a pure engineering choice with a pricing consequence. An asynchronous batch tier, typically priced at about half the synchronous rate in exchange for a delivery window of some hours, is available to any workload the user does not watch: nightly repository scans, overnight report pre-drafting, retrospective quality audits. And a committed-capacity agreement — reserved throughput at a discount in exchange for a monthly minimum — does something more consequential than save money: it changes the shape of your cost curve from linear to step-plus-linear, which changes your optimal pricing. A company whose costs are largely fixed should price for volume and fill capacity; a company whose costs are purely variable should price for margin per unit. Teams routinely sign a committed-capacity deal for the discount and then keep pricing as though every call still costs list, which throws away the strategic half of the benefit.

At sufficient volume, the make-versus-buy line moves, and it moves earlier than most teams expect. Self-hosting an open-weights model on rented GPUs converts inference into a capacity problem: you pay for the hardware whether you use it or not, and your marginal cost per token approaches zero until you saturate, at which point it steps up by one more machine. The break-even against an API is V* = F / (papi − pself), where F is the monthly fixed cost of the cluster and pself is your realised per-token cost at your actual utilisation, which is the term everyone gets wrong: a cluster run at 30% utilisation has a per-token cost more than three times its nameplate.

Ramesh's situation makes the point that the make-versus-buy calculation is not really about money at the margin; it is about who bears the risk of a capability you have promised. A hosted API is a variable cost with a supplier who can change the price, deprecate the model, or change its behaviour in a point release — three distinct risks, of which the third is the one that ruins regulated products. A self-hosted open-weights model is a fixed cost with a version you control absolutely, which is worth a great deal to a company whose model is named in a device submission and nothing at all to a consumer app that would happily take whatever is best this quarter. Cost-to-serve analysis that stops at the rupee figure misses that the two options are not the same product.

4. When the discipline applies, when it binds, and when it actively misleads

It is worth stating the conditions under which cost-to-serve should govern a pricing decision as claims that can be checked, rather than as general good sense. There are five, and each of the two protagonists passes some and fails others, which is why their correct answers differ.

Claim one: the variable cost is material relative to the price of the plan that bears it. The working threshold most practitioners use is that inference above roughly 15% of a plan's price warrants active management and above 30% warrants a pricing change rather than an engineering one, because below 15% the engineering effort has better uses. Bhanwar's paid mid-market plan at $79 per seat per month, with a heavy user consuming perhaps 90 deep reviews, carries $5.30 of inference — 6.7%, comfortably immaterial. Its free tier carries infinity percent of nothing, which is why the claim must be applied plan by plan and never to a company average. Bhrigu fails the claim spectacularly: inference is 346% of the software revenue on the affected contracts. The claim is not a diagnosis, it is a triage rule, and it points Aditi at the free tier alone while pointing Ramesh at the contract itself.

Claim two: usage is correlated with value received, not merely with value delivered. This is the condition under which a usage-linked price is fair and defensible. In Bhanwar's case it holds well: a developer who gets 200 reviews a month is getting roughly 200 units of value, and pricing on review volume would not feel arbitrary. In Bhrigu's case it holds at the level of the health programme — more studies means more tuberculosis detected, which is precisely the value — but it fails at the level of the buying unit, because the state health mission's budget was appropriated per device, not per study, and a per-study charge would require a different budget line, a different approval, and in some cases a different procurement category. Cost-to-serve tells you what a unit costs; it cannot tell you whether your buyer has a mechanism for paying per unit, and in public-sector and regulated buying that mechanism is often the binding constraint.

Claim three: you can observe the cost at the granularity at which you price. This sounds like plumbing and is in fact the most common reason cost-to-serve programmes fail. If you price per seat but can only attribute inference per workspace, you cannot compute the thing you need. Bhanwar could attribute cost per review and per repository, which is why its analysis was possible in an afternoon. Bhrigu could attribute cost per report but not per contract without a join across three systems, because device serial numbers lived in the manufacturing ERP, contracts in the CRM, and inference logs in a cloud project keyed by API token — a three-week data engineering task standing between the company and knowing which customers were unprofitable.

Claim four: the price can move before the cost does damage. This is the claim about optionality and it is the one this page cares about most. A monthly self-serve plan can be repriced with thirty days' notice; an annual enterprise contract with a fixed fee cannot be repriced for up to twelve months; a five-year public-sector contract with an “unlimited” clause cannot be repriced at all. The longer your price commitment relative to the volatility of your cost, the more of a written option you are carrying, and the option is not free merely because no one charged you a premium for it. Aditi passes this claim easily. Ramesh fails it absolutely, and everything he can do now is a workaround for having failed it in November 2024.

Claim five: the quality level is a choice you are permitted to make. Cost-to-serve management assumes you can trade quality for cost at the margin. Where a regulator, a contract or a safety case has fixed the quality point, that lever is gone and the only remaining levers are volume, price and architecture. Bhrigu is the clean illustration: the whole toolkit of model routing and quality degradation, which is the first thing any consultant would propose, is unavailable to it in the cloud reporting path because the model is a named component of a regulated device, while it remains fully available in the unregulated parts of the product, such as the internal quality-audit tooling and the customer-facing analytics summaries. Expert practitioners map the regulated and unregulated surfaces of their product separately for exactly this reason.

And now the inversion, which matters as much as the conditions: there are situations in which cost-to-serve discipline is actively misleading, and recognising them is part of the expertise. The first is when the feature's function is discovery of demand rather than delivery of value — an experimental capability shipped to learn whether anyone wants it, where the right budget is a research budget with a hard stop and a date, and where optimising it is premature by construction. The second is when the variable cost is small relative to a fixed cost that the analysis ignores: a team can spend two engineer-quarters, at perhaps ₹40 lakh fully loaded, to save ₹9 lakh a year of inference, and this happens constantly because inference spend is visible on a dashboard while engineering opportunity cost is not. The third is when cost-to-serve is used as a proxy for whether the feature should exist, which it cannot do in either direction: a nearly-free feature that nobody values is a waste, and an expensive feature that lifts paid conversion by three points is a bargain. The fourth, and subtlest, is in a competitive land-grab where the category's pricing norms are being set right now and a cost-disciplined entrant simply loses the category to someone who is willing to be temporarily irrational — the condition under which the land-and-deflate school is not reckless but correct.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

Multi-product companies fight about allocation, and the fight is not really about allocation. A company with four products drawing on one inference contract must decide how to split a shared bill, and whatever transfer-pricing rule it picks will distort behaviour. Charge each product line its metered consumption at list price and you penalise the team that adopted AI first and most ambitiously, while the committed-use discount the company negotiated accrues to nobody. Charge everyone the blended discounted rate and you have created a commons: each team's marginal cost is below the company's marginal cost at the margin of the commitment, so every team over-consumes. Bhaandar Commerce Cloud, a Gurugram company selling storefront, catalogue, logistics and support products to about 14,000 Indian D2C brands, spent most of 2025 discovering this. Its catalogue team had built a product-description generator that cost ₹0.40 per listing and drove real adoption; its support team had built a chatbot that cost ₹3.10 per resolved ticket and was, on any honest accounting, unprofitable on the entry plan. Because both drew on the same committed contract and the finance team reported a single “AI COGS” line to the board, the catalogue team's efficiency was invisibly subsidising the support team's problem, and the board's view of the company's AI margin was an average of a good business and a bad one. The fix Bhaandar eventually adopted — charge each product line at the marginal rate it would pay standalone, and hold the commitment discount centrally as a treasury gain — is unglamorous and correct, and it took a year because the argument was never about accounting; it was about which general manager had to explain a number.

Two-sided markets must decide which side's inference to subsidise, and the intuitive answer is often wrong. Bhatkanti Journeys, a marketplace connecting travellers with about 22,000 small homestay and guesthouse operators across the Himalayan and Konkan belts, added two AI features in the same quarter: an itinerary assistant for travellers and a listing-and-pricing copilot for hosts. Traveller-side inference cost roughly nine times host-side inference in aggregate, because there are many more travellers and they browse without transacting. The instinct was to cap the traveller feature. The analysis said the opposite: a traveller conversation that ended in a booking generated ₹340 of take rate against ₹11 of inference across the whole session, whereas the host copilot generated no direct revenue at all and was justified only by listing quality, which was hard to attribute. The right question in a two-sided market is never “does this feature pay for itself?” but “does the inference spent on this side increase the volume of transactions on which we earn, net of what it costs on both sides?” What made this hard at Bhatkanti was not the economics but the attribution window: host-side improvements paid back over quarters, traveller-side within days, and the company's monthly cost review naturally favoured whichever side had the shorter feedback loop.

Regulated products lose the cheapest lever. The general case is Bhrigu's: where the model is part of a validated system, model choice becomes a change-control decision with a documentation cost and a timeline measured in months, so the routing playbook is unavailable on the regulated path. The same pattern appears wherever data-residency rules bite — if personal data must remain in India under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act's cross-border provisions, or if a financial customer's data must stay within a regulated boundary, the set of models you may use shrinks to those offered in-region, which are frequently a generation behind and sometimes priced above the global list. A practitioner who quotes a global price list while serving a regulated Indian workload is quoting a price they cannot buy at.

Hardware plus software is where the option written is largest and least visible. A device sold outright with bundled software carries an implicit promise of perpetual service, and a variable cost inside a perpetual promise is an unhedged short position with no expiry. The mature handling is structural rather than clever: separate the hardware price from a software subscription that is annually repriceable; specify the AI service in the contract as a defined quantity ("up to N reports per unit per month, additional reports at ₹X") rather than as an adjective ("unlimited"); and include a technology-substitution clause that permits the vendor to change the underlying model provided it meets a stated performance specification, which converts the model from a named component into a performance obligation. Every one of these is easy to write in year one and impossible to retrofit in year three.

AI-native companies are a different species and should stop pretending otherwise. A company whose entire product is inference has a gross margin structurally in the 40–65% band, not the 80% band, and no amount of optimisation moves it into SaaS territory while the model is rented. The mistake such companies make is not the margin; it is reporting a blended figure that mixes a legacy high-margin product with a new low-margin one, so that the board sees 71% and the incremental margin on everything sold this quarter is 44%. Bhanwar's investor was asking precisely the right question by asking for incremental rather than blended. The related error is allowing inference to sit in R&D as “experimentation” long after it has become production cost, which flatters gross margin while inflating operating expense and postpones the reckoning to whichever quarter the auditors reclassify it.

The organisational seams deserve their own paragraph because they cause more damage than any modelling error. In most companies the inference bill arrives at a cloud or platform team, the pricing decision sits with product or a pricing council, the contract sits with sales, and the P&L sits with finance — and none of these four has both the data and the authority. The diagnostic tell is simple and almost universal: ask who noticed the problem first. If the answer is an accountant during a close, or a platform engineer chasing a budget alert, the seam is open. In the companies that handle this well, the cost per outcome for every AI surface appears on the same weekly product review as activation and retention, owned by the product manager whose feature generates it, with finance present rather than reporting afterwards. That arrangement is rarer than the number of conference talks about it would suggest. What most mature companies actually do, as opposed to what they say, is run a quarterly panic followed by a quarter of discipline, on a cycle, with the amplitude decreasing over about two years as the norms settle.

6. Nine distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

The mean is a summary of the past; the tail is a description of the risk. A competent practitioner computes average cost per session and manages it. An expert asks for the distribution and looks first at the ratio of mean to median, because that ratio is a direct measure of how much of the bill is being written by a minority of interactions. A mean-to-median ratio near one means the cost is a rate and can be budgeted like electricity; a ratio above two means the cost is an insurance exposure and must be capped, reinsured or architecturally bounded. The tell in the wild: a forecast that has been revised upward three months running despite no change in user numbers. The obvious reading is that usage is growing; the correct reading is usually that the sample is growing and therefore reaching further into a tail that was always there.

Cost per token is a supplier metric; cost per accepted outcome is the only one with a business meaning. A competent practitioner optimises the price paid per million tokens. An expert optimises the cost of the work the customer actually keeps, which makes acceptance rate a cost lever of the first order: raising the share of drafts accepted without rework from 58% to 84%, as Bhrigu did, cut the number of wasted generations by nearly two-thirds and would have reduced cost per accepted report even if the per-call price had risen by half. The tell: a team that can tell you their token price to three decimal places and cannot tell you their rejection rate. The obvious reading is that they are cost-disciplined; the correct reading is that they are measuring the input to a process whose yield they have never examined.

“Unlimited” is a short option, and the strike price is set by your own roadmap. When you promise unlimited use at a fixed price, you have sold the customer the right to consume as much as they like at zero marginal price, and the value of that right rises when your product gets better — which is to say, your own success is the event that puts the option in the money. This is the deep reason Bhrigu's contract hurt: the trigger was not customer opportunism but Bhrigu's own decision to improve report quality. The tell: a pricing page whose most confident word is “unlimited” and a roadmap whose next three items all increase per-interaction cost. The obvious reading is that the company is generous; the correct reading is that two documents inside the same company are making opposite bets.

Price declines are indexed to capability, not to tasks, and the two diverge. The claim that inference gets ten times cheaper a year is true when you hold the capability constant and false when you hold the job constant, because the frontier of what teams choose to do has moved from one-shot answers to multi-step agents that consume tens or hundreds of calls, and from short answers to reasoning traces that bill as output. An expert therefore runs two series side by side: the price of a fixed capability over time, which falls, and the company's own realised cost per completed task, which usually does not. The tell: a deck that justifies a pricing decision with a chart of falling token prices and contains no chart of the company's own cost per task. The obvious reading is that the market is deflating in the company's favour; the correct reading is that the company is on an escalator going the other way.

A cap is a product specification, because users optimise against whatever line you draw. The moment a limit exists, behaviour reorganises around it: users batch their questions into one enormous prompt to conserve credits, which raises cost per call while reducing call count; teams create multiple free accounts, which converts a cost problem into an identity-fraud problem; and the heaviest and most engaged users — often the ones who evangelise the product — are precisely the ones who hit the wall. An expert designs the cap as a feature, with a visible counter, a graceful degradation rather than a hard stop, and an upgrade path presented at the moment of frustration rather than after it. The tell: a cap that was implemented in a sprint by the platform team and communicated in a changelog. The obvious reading is that the cost problem is solved; the correct reading is that a pricing change has been shipped without anyone treating it as one.

Free tiers on AI features are arbitraged, and abuse cost is a different distribution again. Any free endpoint with a capable model behind it will, within months, attract automated consumption: resellers wrapping it in their own product, scrapers harvesting outputs to train or evaluate something else, and simple abuse. This traffic is not a fat tail of legitimate use; it is a separate population with different statistics, typically machine-regular in timing and unusually uniform in prompt structure. An expert separates the two populations before computing anything, because mixing them corrupts both the cost forecast and the product judgement drawn from usage data. The tell: free-tier usage that does not dip on Indian festival holidays or at 3 a.m. The obvious reading is global adoption; the correct reading is often a script.

Latency and cost are the same budget spent in different currencies. Every technique that reduces cost — smaller models, cached context, batch tiers, aggressive truncation — changes the latency and the quality profile, and every technique that reduces latency — parallel calls, speculative execution, pre-generation of likely answers — increases cost, often by generating work that is discarded. An expert treats the three as a single constrained optimisation with an explicit trade rate rather than as three separate initiatives owned by three teams. The tell: a company with a latency SLO, a cost dashboard, and a quality eval suite, maintained by different people, whose targets have never been reconciled in one document. The obvious reading is three healthy disciplines; the correct reading is three local optima.

The free tier's real cost is the quality floor it imposes, not the tokens it burns. The cheapest route for a free user is a small model, but a free user is also a prospective customer forming their entire impression of the product's competence from that interaction, and in consumer and product-led businesses the free experience is the marketing. This creates a genuine bind: the tier with the least revenue per interaction is the tier with the highest brand leverage per interaction. Experts resolve it by being generous in quality and stingy in quantity — give the free user the good model for a bounded number of interactions rather than the weak model for unlimited ones — which is also, not coincidentally, the design that makes the upgrade prompt honest. The tell: a cost-reduction plan whose first line is “downgrade the free tier to the compact model” with no accompanying quality measurement. The obvious reading is prudence; the correct reading is an untested bet that the thing bringing users in will survive being made worse.

In Indian-language products, the same sentence costs more, and nobody budgets for it. Tokenisers are trained predominantly on English text, and Indic scripts fragment badly: a sentence in Devanagari, Tamil or Bengali commonly consumes two to four times as many tokens as its English equivalent, and Romanised code-mixed text lands somewhere in between. A product serving a multilingual Indian user base therefore has a cost-to-serve that varies by a factor of three across its own users for identical value delivered, and pricing that ignores this either overcharges the English-speaking metro user or silently makes the vernacular user unprofitable — usually the latter, which is to say the expansion market the company is counting on. The tell: a cost-per-user chart that has never been cut by interface language. The obvious reading is that language is a localisation concern; the correct reading is that language is a unit-economics variable.

7. How the problem changes shape across business models and company stages

The useful way to organise the differences is not by industry label but by the two variables that actually drive the exposure: how long your price is committed for, and how variable your cost per outcome is. Plot any product on those two axes and its correct strategy falls out, which is more than can be said for most segmentation frameworks.

Within that frame, the segment differences are real but narrower than the usual commentary implies. In consumer products the binding constraint is willingness to pay, which is low and lumpy, so the only viable path is architectural: cost per interaction must be engineered down to the point where an advertising or subscription model can carry it, and caps must be generous enough that the median user never perceives them. In B2B mid-market the binding constraint is the sales motion, which cannot tolerate a complicated meter, so the craft lies in building a plan whose included quantity is set at roughly the ninetieth percentile of observed usage with overage priced above cost, giving the buyer predictability and the vendor a tail hedge. In enterprise the constraint is the contract, and the whole game is won or lost in the redlines: defined quantities, annual reprice rights, model-substitution clauses, and a separate line for AI that can be renegotiated without reopening the platform agreement. In platforms and marketplaces the unit of analysis is the transaction rather than the interaction, and the correct denominator is take-rate revenue per unit of inference across both sides, as at Bhatkanti. In hardware the danger is the perpetual promise, and the fix is structural separation of device and service. In AI-native products, where the model is the product, none of this is a feature-level concern at all — it is the company's cost structure, and it belongs in the strategy, not in a pricing review.

Where the difference is genuinely smaller than people claim is between B2B and enterprise: both have identified buyers, both can meter, and the real distinction is contract length rather than anything about the product. And the most overstated difference is between AI features and any other capacity-constrained service business — a hospital, an airline, a law firm. Those industries solved variable cost-to-serve decades ago with defined scopes, overage rates, peak pricing and utilisation management, and much of what looks novel in AI pricing is a rediscovery of their playbook by people who have never had to read it.

Stage changes the answer as much as segment does. A pre-product-market-fit company should deliberately overspend on inference, because the information it buys about what users want is worth more than the money, provided there is a hard ceiling and a named date. A company at early scale — Bhanwar's position — faces the characteristic transition: the thing that must change is not the bill but the instrumentation, because at this stage the company is about to sign contracts and publish pricing that will be hard to unwind. A growth-stage company gains two new levers, committed capacity and its own distilled or fine-tuned models, and acquires one new failure mode, which is that the team now optimises the cost of a product architecture nobody has revisited in a year. And a mature company's constraint is almost never technical: it is the installed base of contracts and expectations that makes any change a migration, which is why the mature company's most valuable asset in this domain is a contract template written by someone who understood the problem before the company had it.

8. Three worked examples, including one that failed

Example one: Bhanwar Systems bounds the tail without touching the median

Aditi's team ran three options against the August distribution before the board meeting. Option A, moving the free tier to the compact model, would have cut free-tier spend from $79,900 to about $9,400 — but an offline evaluation on 500 sampled reviews showed the helpful-rating rate falling from 71% to 44%, below even the old shallow reviewer, because the compact model could not follow multi-file reasoning. Given that the free tier was the company's entire acquisition channel, the team judged this a 88% saving purchased with an unknown but plausibly larger reduction in conversion. Option B, a hard monthly cap of twenty deep reviews per free repository, landed near the p95 point of Table 3 and saved 38%. Option C, which is what they chose, was an architectural bound rather than a usage cap: a per-review budget of 25,000 input tokens and 12 agent steps for free repositories, above which the agent stops exploring, writes its review from what it has, and appends a single line noting that the diff was large enough to warrant the paid deep review. That change removed 41% of free-tier spend, truncated the maximum possible review cost at $0.34 from $31.70, and affected the review content of 6.2% of free reviews while leaving 93.8% byte-identical. It also produced an upgrade prompt that appeared exactly when the product had visibly reached a limit, which converted at 4.4% against the 0.9% of the generic banner it replaced.

The instructive part is the comparison between B and C. Both save roughly the same money. A usage cap rations the number of good experiences a free user may have; an architectural budget rations the depth of each experience while keeping the number unlimited. For a product whose free tier exists to demonstrate competence, the second is strictly better, and the two look identical on a cost spreadsheet. That is the kind of judgement a spreadsheet cannot make for you.

Example two: Bhaandar Commerce Cloud reprices around the value metric

Bhaandar's support chatbot cost ₹3.10 per resolved ticket against an entry plan at ₹4,999 a month that included unlimited support automation, and merchants on that plan averaged 1,900 resolved tickets a month during the festive quarter — ₹58,900 of inference against ₹4,999 of revenue on the worst cohort. The company's first instinct was a cap. Its pricing lead instead changed the value metric: support automation moved out of the platform plan and became a separate module priced at ₹11 per resolved ticket, with resolution defined as a ticket closed without human escalation within 24 hours — a definition that made Bhaandar's own quality the condition of getting paid. Merchants were offered a comparison against their existing agency and in-house agent costs, which ran between ₹40 and ₹90 per ticket. Adoption of the module reached 61% of the eligible base within two quarters; the merchants who declined were disproportionately the ones whose ticket volume had been unprofitable. Gross margin on the module settled at 72%. The lesson is the value-metric school's central claim in its strongest form: the cost problem dissolved not because the cost changed but because the unit of sale finally matched the unit of consumption, and because the new metric was one the customer could already price against an alternative.

Example three: Bhavtaal Learning, where it went wrong and what recovery actually cost

Bhavtaal Learning, a Jaipur company selling board-exam preparation to students in Classes 9 to 12, launched an AI doubt-solving tutor in June 2025 on a freemium model: unlimited doubts for everyone, with a ₹399-a-month paid tier adding mock tests, analytics and parent reports. The feature was an immediate success, and the company's free-to-paid conversion rose from 3.1% to 5.4% — a genuine, well-measured improvement that justified the build. Three things then compounded. First, seasonality: doubt volume between December and February, as board exams approached, ran at 4.2 times the October baseline, because the product's usage peak coincided exactly with its users' anxiety peak. Second, language: 71% of doubts arrived in Hindi or Hinglish, which, per the tokenisation asymmetry above, cost roughly 1.6 to 2.4 times an English doubt, a fact nobody had modelled because the pilot cohort had been an English-medium school in Jaipur. Third, and most damaging, image input: students photographed textbook problems rather than typing them, so 78% of doubts arrived as images requiring a multimodal model at several times the text price. January 2026's inference bill was ₹2.31 crore against monthly revenue of ₹1.04 crore.

Three details of the recovery deserve attention because they are where the real work was. The largest single saving was not the model swap but an OCR pre-pass: instead of sending every photograph to a multimodal model, Bhavtaal ran a cheap optical character recognition step, sent the extracted text to a text-only model, and escalated to the multimodal model only when the OCR confidence was low or the problem contained a diagram — which applied to 23% of images. That one architectural change cut cost per doubt by 58% with no measurable change in answer quality. The second saving came from a distilled model: Bhavtaal fine-tuned a small open-weights model on 140,000 of its own accepted answers, at a one-time cost of about ₹21 lakh including engineering, and used it for the roughly 60% of doubts that were routine chapters-one-to-four material, escalating the rest. The third change was not technical at all: caps were replaced with a daily allowance of credits that refilled, were visible, could be earned by completing practice sets, and were framed as a study mechanic rather than a restriction. Same truncation of the distribution, entirely different meaning to a sixteen-year-old. The company's own retrospective concluded that the failure had not been the unlimited free tier — which had, after all, doubled conversion — but the absence of any instrument that would have shown cost per doubt by language and input type before December, and the absence of a pre-agreed plan for what to do when the number moved.

9. Failure modes, their early warning signs, and the cost of catching them late

The failures in this domain are unusually legible in hindsight and unusually easy to miss in the moment, because each of them looks, at the time, like a team doing its job well. What follows is the set that recurs, with the signal that appears before the damage and the question that would have surfaced it.

Two of these deserve more than a row. The first is silent quality degradation, because it is the failure mode with the worst ratio of damage to visibility. When a team routes traffic to a cheaper model and measures only cost, the saving appears immediately and in full, while the harm appears slowly, diffusely, and in metrics owned by someone else — a slightly lower activation rate, a slightly higher support volume, a slow drift in app store sentiment. By the time anyone connects the two, the engineer who made the change has moved teams and the causal chain is unrecoverable. The discipline that prevents it is unromantic: no model change ships without a held-out evaluation set and a stated acceptance-rate threshold, and the cost saving is reported alongside the quality delta in the same document, every time, including when the delta is zero.

The second is the attribution gap, because it is the failure that makes all the others harder to fix. A company that cannot join inference spend to accounts cannot compute per-customer margin, cannot identify which contracts to renegotiate, cannot tell abuse from enthusiasm, and cannot answer the investor question that Bhanwar's board member asked. The work to close it is a week or two of tagging — propagating an account identifier through to every model call and into the billing export — and it is almost always deprioritised because it produces no user-visible value. It is the single highest-return week of engineering available to most companies in this situation, and the reason to do it early is that its value is greatest precisely when you are too busy to build it.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Whether to price to today's cost or tomorrow's. The deflationists hold that the cost of a fixed capability falls by roughly an order of magnitude a year, that this has held for three consecutive years across multiple vendors, and that pricing to today's cost therefore means pricing yourself out of a market you would have owned. They can point to companies that priced defensively in 2023, lost the category, and now have excellent gross margins on a small business. The margin-restoration camp replies that the deflation is real but is captured by the customer only if the vendor holds capability constant, that no ambitious product team does so, and that a company burning capital against a future cost curve is making a leveraged bet on a supply market it does not control — one price increase, one model deprecation, one capacity shortage, and the thesis inverts. The disagreement is empirically resolvable in principle: track your own realised cost per completed task for eighteen months. If it has fallen, the deflationists were right for your product. In most agentic products it has risen. What would have to be true for the deflationists to be right in general is that product teams become willing to hold quality constant and bank the savings, and there is very little evidence that they do.

Whether AI application companies should be metered at all. The consumption camp argues that a variable cost demands a variable price, that customers already accept metering from cloud providers and telecoms, and that any other structure forces the vendor to carry usage risk it cannot control — and points out that flat pricing on variable cost systematically transfers value from light users to heavy ones, which is a subsidy the vendor did not intend. The flat-pricing camp argues that metering suppresses exactly the behaviour a young product needs most — exploratory use — that procurement departments in large enterprises structurally prefer a predictable number and will pay a premium of twenty to thirty percent for it, and that the evidence from a decade of cloud cost-management anxiety is that customers hate meters even when they are fair. The synthesis usually proposed — a flat plan with an included quantity and overage — is not a synthesis so much as a compromise that inherits both problems: it has a meter, so it suppresses exploration near the limit, and it has a flat component, so it carries usage risk below the limit. Reasonable people place the threshold in different places and do not agree.

Whether gross margin is destiny for AI-native companies. One position holds that a 50% gross margin business is simply a different and less valuable kind of company than an 80% one, that the market will eventually price it as such, and that pretending otherwise is a category error dressed as optimism. The opposing position holds that gross margin in a young industry is a lagging indicator of an immature supply chain, points to the history of cloud hosting and of e-commerce logistics, where margins improved by twenty points over a decade as scale and vertical integration arrived, and argues that a company with a defensible position and improving unit economics should not sacrifice growth to a ratio that is mechanically improving anyway. What would falsify the optimistic view is a plateau: two or three years in which realised cost per delivered outcome stops falling because capability demands rise as fast as efficiency does. Some categories already show that plateau. Others do not.

Whether to degrade quality silently. This is the sharpest ethical disagreement in the field and it is rarely conducted openly. One camp holds that the model serving a request is an implementation detail, like which data centre serves a page, and that vendors owe customers an outcome specification rather than a component list. The other holds that when the product's entire value is the quality of a generated judgement, the model is not an implementation detail but the product, and that swapping it without disclosure — particularly downward, and particularly for the non-paying tier whose experience is the basis of a purchase decision — is a misrepresentation. The practical test that separates them is whether you would be comfortable if the change were published in the release notes. Many companies that would defend the first position in the abstract do not publish, which tells you something.

Whether to self-host. The integration camp argues that inference is a core cost of goods, that owning the model stack is the only route to durable margin and to the version stability that regulated and enterprise customers require, and that the break-even volume arrives earlier than most teams believe. The rental camp argues that the frontier moves faster than any single company can follow, that owning weights means owning an asset that depreciates in months, that utilisation risk is real and underestimated, and that engineering attention spent on inference infrastructure is attention not spent on the product. Both are right about different companies, and the variable that decides it is not volume but whether model version stability is worth money to your customers. For Bhrigu it is worth a great deal. For Bhanwar it is worth nothing at all.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this topic can compute a cost per call, name the levers, and recommend a cap. Someone who has internalised it behaves differently in six observable ways, and the differences show up before there is a problem rather than after.

They ask about the tail first. Handed a new AI feature proposal, their first question is not what it costs but what the worst case costs and what enforces it — and they ask it during design review, when the answer is a two-line change, rather than during a cost review, when the answer is a migration. They treat an unbounded loop the way a database engineer treats an unbounded query: not as a cost risk but as a correctness defect.

They write the commitment before they write the price. Before a pricing page or a contract schedule is drafted, they establish how long the company is committing for and what mechanism exists to change it — the reprice right, the defined quantity, the substitution clause — because they know from experience that the pricing number can be fixed in a quarter and the commitment structure cannot be fixed at all. In practice this means they are unusually interested in sales contract templates for a product person, and unusually willing to make an enemy of a sales leader in September to avoid a board conversation in March.

They keep two cost series, not one. The vendor price list and their own realised cost per accepted outcome, plotted together, because they know the gap between the two is the measure of how much efficiency their own organisation is consuming internally. When the two diverge, they do not treat it as a finance question; they treat it as evidence about their own team's habits.

They know their generosity budget as a number. They can say, without looking it up, what a free user is worth in expected gross profit and therefore what the company is entitled to spend serving one. This turns the free-tier argument from a values debate — growth people want generosity, finance people want discipline — into an arithmetic one, and it is remarkable how quickly a meeting improves when someone puts the justified budget on the table and asks whether the current spend is above or below it.

They distinguish rationing quantity from rationing depth, and they usually choose depth. Because they understand that a free tier's job is to demonstrate competence, they would rather bound how thoroughly each interaction is served than how many interactions a user may have, and they design the boundary so that reaching it is informative rather than punitive — the moment where the user learns what the paid product does.

And they are calm about the bill and alarmed about the instrument. A large inference bill on a feature that is measurably driving conversion does not worry them; an inability to cut that bill by language, by input type, by account and by percentile worries them a great deal, because they have seen that every recovery in this domain begins with the same three weeks of data work, and that the companies that suffer least are the ones that did those three weeks while nothing was on fire.

12. What the two protagonists decided

Aditi Kulkarni presented three things to the Bhanwar board on 26 September. The free tier stayed, unlimited in number of reviews, because the analysis showed it was 55% over its justified budget rather than catastrophically mispriced and because it remained the company's only meaningful acquisition channel. It gained an architectural budget — twelve agent steps, 25,000 input tokens, a hard stop — which cut spend 41% and capped the maximum single review at $0.34. Paid plans gained the unbounded agent as an explicit, named feature rather than an accident of implementation, which is what made the free tier's limit legible as a product boundary rather than a cost measure. And she brought the incremental-margin table her investor had asked for, showing 81% on the mid-market plan including allocated free-tier cost, alongside a commitment to report it monthly. The reasoning she gave was the one this page has been building toward: the company had not had a cost problem, it had had an unbounded liability that nobody had authorised, and the fix was to bound it in the architecture rather than in the pricing page, because the architecture could be changed without asking users to accept less.

Ramesh Iyer had no equivalently clean move available, which is the point of including him. His recommendation to Bhrigu's board had four parts, none of them satisfying. First, accelerate the self-hosting migration, on the break-even in Fig. 2, accepting two quarters of dual-running cost and the regulatory work of demonstrating weight equivalence — a project whose business case was entirely the ₹37 lakh a month it would save on current volume. Second, build a two-stage reporting path in which the cheaper first-stage labels drive a structured template for routine normal studies, escalating to the expensive multimodal drafter only for flagged or ambiguous ones — a change that required a regulatory amendment and clinical sign-off, and which the clinical team resisted on the reasonable ground that the abnormal studies are not the only ones where a missed finding matters. Third, approach the two state health missions not to reopen price, which he judged both futile and reputationally costly, but to propose an expansion in which new units are contracted on a defined-quantity schedule, so that growth at least stops making the problem worse. Fourth, and the only cost-free item, rewrite the contract template: defined quantities, annual reprice on the software line, and a model-substitution clause defining the obligation as a performance specification rather than a named component. He noted in the paper, with some bitterness, that the fourth item would have prevented the first three.

Discussion questions

  1. Bhanwar chose an architectural budget over a usage cap and reported that 93.8% of free reviews were unchanged. Suppose instead the figure had been 70%. At what level of altered experience does an architectural bound stop being an engineering decision and become a pricing change requiring the same review, communication and measurement as a change to the price list? Who in the company should own that threshold?
  2. Bhrigu's cost crisis was caused by a quality improvement that the clinical evidence supported and that patients benefited from. If you were on Bhrigu's board, would you approve a return to the cheaper model for routine studies in order to protect the company's ability to serve the contract at all — and how would you want that trade-off documented to the state health missions, if at all?
  3. Bhavtaal recovered by replacing caps with earnable credits, which truncated the same distribution while being received entirely differently. Is the difference between the two a legitimate exercise of product craft, or is it a framing device that obscures a reduction in what the customer receives? Would your answer change if the users were procurement officers rather than sixteen-year-olds?
